kuhn.citation: Kuhn, H. W. (1950). A simplified two-person poker. In Kuhn, H. W. and Tucker, A. W. (eds.), Contributions to the Theory of Games, volume 1, pages 97–103. Princeton University Press.
kuhn.notes: Net chip value for the first player at equilibrium. Showdown pays the current stake to the higher card. A fold loses one chip. This constant is not derived from the Paignia trainer. At the listed budgets an independent deal enumerator checks that both variants stay within 5e-3 of this value and that exploitability shrinks. The value error itself is not monotone, and these budgets are not a published training curve.

leduc.citation: Southey, F., Bowling, M., Larson, B., Piccione, C., Burch, N., Billings, D., and Rayner, C. (2005). Bayes' bluff: opponent modelling in poker. Proceedings of the 21st Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, pages 550-558. The extensive form follows the two-player OpenSpiel leduc_poker defaults: six distinguishable cards, ante 1, raise sizes 2 and 4, and a two-raise cap.
leduc.notes: First-player equilibrium value reproduced for this rule set. It is not a closed form and was not taken from the Paignia trainer. The check-check showdown value is checked by a separate 120-deal ranking loop. Vanilla CFR and CFR+ are both compared at 1,000 and 4,000 iterations, and Nash conv is smaller at 4,000. The published value is checked only for CFR+ at 4,000 iterations. This is not an exact equilibrium and not a published iteration curve.
